endorsements.quote: Other risks to consider include human factors that might lead to misuse of the AI tool (eg, not following the instructions, receiving insufficient training), application of the AI tool to individuals who are not within the target population, use of the tool by others than the target end users (eg, technician instead of physician)

evidence.title: Influence of medical educational background on the diagnostic quality of ChatGPT-4 responses in internal medicine: A pilot study
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic ranking quality of ChatGPT-4 responses by user expertise level
evidence.effect: Residents significantly outperformed students (OR 2.33, p = .007); overall diagnostic performance was low.
evidence.quote: Diagnostic ranking, assessed by independent experts, revealed that residents significantly outperformed students (OR 2.33, p = .007); though overall performance was low.
evidence.sample_unit: participants (third-year students, residents, specialists) summarising five NEJM cases

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether assessing misuse, user-error, and task-related risk, or raising the risk tier when intended users lack the needed expertise, reduces misinterpretation or off-target use. The recommendation rests on regulatory and consensus guidance, along with one simulated study showing that output quality varied with user expertise.

perspectives.view: No study evaluated the practice itself. The single related study is a level 4 cross-sectional simulation that documents the hazard and does not test any risk-tiering procedure. Under GRADE conventions, certainty for the practice cannot be rated above no direct evidence, and the hazard finding offers only indirect support for the premise.

In a simulated task, residents ranked ChatGPT-4 diagnoses better than students did (OR 2.33, p = .007), and diagnostic performance was low for both groups. This suggests that the same tool may produce different results depending on who uses it. Whether a higher risk tier would catch these errors before they reach patients has not been studied.

FDA draft guidance says risks from user error should be calculated in both normal and fault conditions. A discussion paper proposes moving patient-facing functions higher on the consequences axis. FUTURE-AI lists insufficient training, use outside the target population, and use by non-target users as risks to assess. These sources describe expectations, and none reports outcomes.

The expertise gradient in the simulated study was measured between two trainee groups using one general-purpose model offline. Its findings may not carry over to deployed tools, to nurses or patients, or to real workflows. No study describes how assessors would judge user expertise in practice or how much work that judgment would add.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare deployments whose risk assessments explicitly account for user expertise and misuse scenarios against deployments whose assessments do not. These studies should measure misinterpretation rates, off-target use, and patient harm in live settings with patient-facing and non-physician users.
commentary.underserved_note: The one hazard study did not report participant or patient demographics, and no study tested the practice. No evidence therefore covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. These groups may be the users most likely to lack the expertise that safe use requires, and the gap may matter most for patient-facing tools.
